issues.legal_issue: The terms of a customary insurance policy govern an accepted insurance contract even when the formal policy has not been delivered.
material_facts: The insurer accepted proposals to insure buildings against fire and specified additional risks, and its acceptance letters referred to cover notes.
The cover notes made the insurance subject to the proposal and the usual conditions of the insurer’s policies.
The insurer had not delivered formal policies before cancelling the cover, and the buildings were later destroyed.
issues.conclusion: A contract of insurance had come into being, and the customary policy terms, including the cancellation condition, governed the parties’ relationship despite the policy not having been issued or delivered.
issues.legal_principle: An insurance contract is formed by unqualified acceptance, and commercial documents such as proposals, acceptance letters, and cover notes must be read together in light of commercial practice. Where the contract is complete but the policy is undelivered, the parties’ rights are governed by the policy intended to issue; customary policy terms apply if the contract does not specify them. The Court relied on the general rule stated in Corpus Juris Secundum, Eames v. Home Insurance Co., General Accident Insurance Corporation v. Cronk, and the principles discussed in Macgillivray on Insurance Law.

predicates.insurance_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns the terms governing an insurance contract.
predicates.accepted_insurance_proposal: The insurer accepted a proposal to provide insurance.
predicates.cover_note_refers_to_customary_policy_te: The cover note referred to the usual terms or conditions of the insurer’s policy.

issues.definition: When an insurer accepts an insurance proposal and the cover note refers to customary policy terms, those terms govern the contract even before formal policy delivery.

issues.legal_issue: A customary insurance condition giving both the insurer and the insured a right to terminate the insurance is not unreasonable merely because it permits termination at will.
material_facts: The cover notes incorporated the usual conditions of the insurer’s policies.
The customary fire policy allowed either the insured or the insurer to terminate the insurance, with a proportionate premium adjustment in the insurer’s case.
The insurer relied on that condition to cancel the cover.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation condition was a usual and reasonable term because it gave both parties a right to terminate the insurance.
issues.legal_principle: Where the parties agree to reciprocal cancellation rights, a court should not make a different contract for them merely because one party may exercise the right at will. The Court relied on Sun Fire Office v. Hart and The Central Bank of India v. Hartford Fire Insurance Co. Ltd., which treated comparable cancellation terms as common and reasonable. It also rejected the argument, based on Sze Hai Tong Bank Ltd. v. Rambler Cycle Co. Ltd., that the condition should be cut down by an implied limitation in these circumstances.

predicates.insurance_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns a term governing termination of an insurance contract.
predicates.cancellation_condition_gives_both_sides_: The contract’s cancellation condition gave both the insurer and the insured a right to terminate the insurance.

issues.definition: A cancellation condition is reasonable when it gives both sides to an insurance contract a right to terminate.

issues.legal_issue: An insurer may validly cancel insurance under a cancellation condition before the insured loss has begun or become inevitable.
material_facts: The insurer cancelled the cover while the insured buildings remained several hundred feet from the river.
The river had risen, but the evidence did not establish that erosion had begun to threaten the buildings or that their destruction was inevitable when the insurer cancelled the cover.
The buildings were washed away later.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation was valid because the evidence did not show that the loss had begun or become inevitable when the insurer cancelled the cover.
issues.legal_principle: A cancellation condition permits cancellation of future risk, but not avoidance of liability for a loss already underway or a risk already turning into a loss. Whether cancellation is legitimate depends on the facts of each case; cancellation is possible before liability has commenced or become inevitable. The Court applied Sun Fire Office v. Hart and The Central Bank of India v. Hartford Fire Insurance Co. Ltd.

predicates.insurance_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns an insurer’s cancellation of insurance cover.
predicates.policy_contains_cancellation_condition: The governing insurance terms included a condition permitting cancellation.
predicates.cancellation_precedes_commenced_or_inevi: When the insurer cancelled the cover, the insured loss had not begun and was not shown to be inevitable.

issues.definition: An insurer’s cancellation is valid when the governing terms permit cancellation and the insurer acts before the insured loss has begun or become inevitable.
